lines.watchItem: Advanced-packaging allocation is the gate on how much accelerator revenue can actually ship: CoWoS is booked out with 52-78 week lead times into 2027 even as monthly capacity climbs toward 125,000-130,000 wafers and the gap narrows from about 20% to about 10%. Watch whether the gap keeps closing or demand refills it.

Packaging demand rests on very few names: the top three CoWoS customers take over 85% of output, with one at roughly 60%. Any single one slowing orders leaves slots that are hard to refill, so watch order patterns from the largest two buyers.

Wafer-start planning faces demand that keeps being revised up: the four largest US cloud buyers are tracking toward roughly $725 billion of 2026 capex, Alphabet lifted guidance twice, and Meta plans 7 gigawatts this year and about double next year. Watch whether these guidance revisions keep pointing the same way.

Leading-node customer mix is shifting from one dominant buyer toward several: merchant-GPU share is projected to fall from 87% in 2024 to about 75% in 2026 while custom AI chips grow 44.6% versus 16.1% for merchant GPUs and AMD lands gigawatt-scale commitments. Watch the split between merchant-GPU and custom-silicon wafer demand.

Pricing power across the chain sits with whoever is scarcest, and right now that is packaging and memory: TSMC's gross margin reached 67.7% with full-year growth guidance raised above 40%, while memory makers post 87% data-center gross margins and HBM4 contract prices are forecast to roughly double into 2027. Watch whether memory pricing starts eating into system budgets.

Stacked memory now caps accelerator output alongside packaging: it is sold out through 2026 with much of 2027 pre-booked, Micron says it can meet only half to two-thirds of demand, and a single supplier holds 56.4% of the market. Watch whether memory, not packaging, becomes the limit that decides shipped units.

Policy and enforcement keep moving the addressable market around: China licensing shifted to case-by-case review for H200-class parts with a 25% tariff and a cap under half of US sales, yet actual shipments stay trivial and NVIDIA's China revenue halved. Watch whether approved licenses ever convert into volume.

Part of the demand signal is being funded rather than earned: NVIDIA raised $25 billion in bonds to backstop roughly 210,000 GPUs at smaller clouds, CoreWeave carries a 5.4:1 debt-to-equity ratio, and Alphabet posted its first negative free cash flow. Watch how much of the order book depends on supplier credit and borrowing.
